He is a former smoker (quit at age 40 after a 10 pack-year history) and drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week socially. He takes no regular medications other than sumatriptan on demand. results.title: CADASIL: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy
results.authors: Chabriat H, Joutel A, Dichgans M, et al.
results.key_finding: CADASIL is caused by mutations in NOTCH3 (chromosome 19p13) and is the most common hereditary cause of ischemic stroke and vascular dementia in adults. Onset of transient ischemic attacks or strokes typically occurs between ages 45-65. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are universal and often precede clinical symptoms; anterior temporal pole involvement on MRI is a highly characteristic feature that helps distinguish CADASIL from hypertensive small vessel disease. External capsule involvement is similarly characteristic.

results.title: MRI white matter lesion topography in CADASIL: a study with high-resolution 3T imaging
results.authors: Dichgans M, Filippi M, Bruning R, et al.
results.key_finding: Anterior temporal pole WMH (sensitivity 89%, specificity 86% for CADASIL vs other WMH etiologies) and external capsule WMH are imaging biomarkers that, in combination with family history and clinical features, strongly support CADASIL diagnosis. NOTCH3 gene sequencing or skin biopsy with electron microscopy (granular osmiophilic material, GOM) confirm the diagnosis.

results.title: European Stroke Organisation guidelines for the management of cerebral small vessel disease
results.authors: Pantoni L et al. (ESO Small Vessel Disease Working Group)
results.key_finding: In patients with stroke or TIA and white matter hyperintensities disproportionate for age — particularly with anterior temporal lobe involvement — and a positive family history of early stroke or dementia, genetic evaluation for CADASIL (NOTCH3 sequencing) should be considered. Antiplatelet therapy is recommended for secondary prevention of ischemic events in CADASIL.

output.summary: CADASIL (NOTCH3 on chromosome 19p13) is the most common hereditary small vessel disease causing lacunar stroke and vascular dementia in middle-aged adults. Characteristic MRI features include subcortical lacunar infarcts and white matter hyperintensities with predominant involvement of the anterior temporal poles and external capsule — distinguishing CADASIL from common hypertensive microangiopathy. Mean age of first stroke is approximately 49 years. Migraine with aura is the most frequent initial symptom (in 20-40% of patients) and may precede stroke by years. Family history of early dementia and stroke in a first-degree relative in an autosomal dominant pattern is a key diagnostic clue. NOTCH3 sequencing confirms diagnosis. No disease-modifying treatment; secondary prevention with antiplatelet therapy and vascular risk factor management is standard.

output.query: IV tPA thrombolysis small vessel lacunar stroke CADASIL antiplatelet secondary prevention

results.title: AHA/ASA 2019 Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, Ackerson T, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) is indicated for eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of last known well time regardless of presumed mechanism. NIHSS >25 is a relative exclusion for IV tPA; small lacunar strokes (NIHSS 0-5) may benefit but evidence is less robust. CT to exclude hemorrhage must precede tPA.

results.title: Stroke prevention in CADASIL: current evidence and practice
results.journal: Journal of Cerebrovascular and Endovascular Neurology
results.key_finding: There is no evidence that IV thrombolysis is contraindicated in CADASIL per se; the diagnosis of CADASIL does not change the acute treatment algorithm. For secondary prevention, antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) is recommended; anticoagulation is not indicated in the absence of atrial fibrillation. Statins for LDL reduction, and aggressive blood pressure management are secondary prevention cornerstones.

output.proposed: Aspirin 100 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily for secondary stroke prevention; sumatriptan (current medication)
interactions: Aspirin + sumatriptan: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both agents may be used together.
Atorvastatin: No significant interaction with aspirin or sumatriptan at standard doses.
contraindications: Sumatriptan is contraindicated in patients with known ischemic heart disease, prior myocardial infarction, or uncontrolled hypertension — coronary vasospastic effects. Current evaluation for cardiac source should inform continued use.
Sumatriptan should not be co-administered with MAO inhibitors or within 24 hours of ergotamine derivatives.
warnings: Aspirin: increased bleeding risk with concurrent NSAIDs; avoid ibuprofen co-administration
Atorvastatin: myopathy risk increased with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, clarithromycin); monitor for myalgia
If clopidogrel selected instead of aspirin: no interaction with sumatriptan or atorvastatin
Sumatriptan: confirm no ischemic heart disease before resuming given acute stroke presentation
alternatives: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily — alternative antiplatelet if aspirin not tolerated
Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) may be considered short-term per AHA/ASA 2019 minor stroke guidelines

findings.result: Heterozygous pathogenic missense variant detected: c.397C>T, p.(Arg133Cys) in exon 4 of NOTCH3. This variant affects a cysteine residue in EGF-like repeat 3 of the NOTCH3 extracellular domain.
findings.reference: Not detected in unaffected population controls. Listed in ClinVar as pathogenic (ClinVar ID: VCV000012345). Present in multiple published CADASIL pedigrees.

findings.result: Pathogenic — ACMG/AMP criteria: PS1 (same amino acid change as established pathogenic variant), PM2 (absent from controls), PP1 (co-segregation in family with CADASIL phenotype per family history), PP3 (multiple computational predictors support pathogenicity).

output.impression: Heterozygous pathogenic NOTCH3 variant c.397C>T, p.(Arg133Cys) detected — an established cysteine-altering mutation in EGF-like repeat 3 of the NOTCH3 extracellular domain. This variant has been reported in multiple CADASIL-affected individuals and pedigrees. Clinical correlation and genetic counseling recommended.
recommended_actions: Clinical correlation and genetic counseling recommended.
Family members at risk may benefit from predictive genetic testing.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (2 hours before arrival) and administer IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) within 4.5 hours if no contraindications are identified on CT and labs
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision

Obtain brain MRI with DWI to confirm acute infarct and characterise white matter lesion topography — anterior temporal pole and external capsule involvement in a young patient with family history should raise suspicion for CADASIL
Complete TOAST-classification workup: ECG, echocardiogram, Holter, carotid imaging, and hypercoagulability screen to exclude cardioembolic and large artery mechanisms
Order NOTCH3 genetic panel when MRI pattern (anterior temporal WMH, external capsule, deep lacunar infarcts) plus autosomal dominant family history of early stroke/dementia is identified
Provide genetic counseling referral and discuss cascade testing for first-degree relatives if NOTCH3 pathogenic variant is confirmed
Do not prescribe anticoagulation for secondary prevention in the absence of atrial fibrillation — antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) is standard for CADASIL
Manage modifiable vascular risk factors: initiate high-intensity statin for LDL reduction; blood pressure monitoring and treatment as indicated
Reassess sumatriptan safety after cardiac workup is complete — triptan use requires exclusion of ischemic heart disease
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not administer IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, or other guideline-listed contraindications are present

Do not initiate anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC, or heparin) for secondary stroke prevention in CADASIL without confirmed atrial fibrillation — anticoagulation is not indicated and may increase bleeding risk in leukoencephalopathy
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below the treatment threshold in the acute phase — risks worsening perfusion to the penumbra
Do not resume sumatriptan before cardiac evaluation excludes ischemic heart disease — triptans are contraindicated in coronary artery disease
key_reasoning_points: Acute lacunar infarct in a 47-year-old with NIHSS 4 and onset within 4.5 hours is within the IV tPA window — non-contrast CT first is the critical first step regardless of suspected hereditary etiology

Bilateral symmetric FLAIR white matter hyperintensities with prominent anterior temporal lobe and external capsule involvement in a patient under 55 years are not characteristic of hypertensive microangiopathy — this topographic pattern is a hallmark of CADASIL and should prompt genetic evaluation

Autosomal dominant family history of early stroke and dementia (mother and brother) in a first-degree pedigree is a major diagnostic clue for CADASIL; this distinguishes it from sporadic small vessel disease

Migraine history (especially migraine with aura in CADASIL families) is the most common initial symptom of CADASIL, often preceding stroke by a decade — but migraine alone is an extremely common condition and should not anchor diagnosis without imaging and family history integration

TOAST classification drives management: completing the full embolic workup (ECG, Holter, echo, carotid imaging) is required before attributing any lacunar stroke to hereditary small vessel disease — cardioembolic and large artery causes must be systematically excluded
CADASIL does not itself contraindicate IV thrombolysis; the same acute stroke protocol applies while the genetic mechanism is being investigated

Secondary prevention in CADASIL is antiplatelet-based (aspirin or clopidogrel); anticoagulation should not be started without confirmed atrial fibrillation — distinction from cardioembolic stroke prevention is clinically important

metadata.real_seed_note: Seed case: Goh et al., Cureus 2023 Oct;15(10):e46482 (PMID 37927774, PMC10624329, CC-BY). 41-year-old male with CADASIL confirmed by NOTCH3 c.397C>T p.(Arg133Cys), presenting with left-sided weakness and ataxia; right corona radiata acute infarct; bilateral anterior temporal and frontal-parietal FLAIR WMH; normal CTA; positive family history (mother and brother with CADASIL). RP05 adapts demographic to 47-year-old White European male (distinct from existing batch), lateralises to left corona radiata causing right-sided deficits, adds explicit migraine history (classic CADASIL feature), adds red herrings (migraine, dyslipidaemia, admission BP), and constructs a full 12-tool trajectory.
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: middle-aged man with acute lacunar infarct in whom the standard embolic workup is entirely negative; the key diagnostic challenge is recognising the characteristic MRI white matter topography (anterior temporal lobe + external capsule FLAIR WMH) plus autosomal dominant family history as pointing to CADASIL, then ordering NOTCH3 genetic panel to confirm. Three grounded red herrings (migraine, mild dyslipidaemia, admission BP) create plausible alternative anchors.
clinical_pearls: Anterior temporal pole WMH on FLAIR MRI is the most specific imaging biomarker for CADASIL — it is rarely seen in hypertensive small vessel disease and should always prompt hereditary arteriopathy evaluation in a young or middle-aged patient

Migraine (particularly with aura) is the first clinical manifestation of CADASIL in 20-40% of patients and may antedate stroke by a decade; migraine alone does not make the diagnosis, but in combination with imaging and family history it is a strong clue
Autosomal dominant pattern of early stroke and dementia in a first-degree relative is the most important clinical discriminator between CADASIL and common sporadic small vessel disease
CADASIL does not contraindicate IV thrombolysis; acute treatment follows standard AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines while genetic confirmation is pending
Secondary prevention in CADASIL is antiplatelet-based; starting anticoagulation without confirmed AF in a patient with leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) may increase intracerebral hemorrhage risk
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools including genetic panel; 3 grounded red herrings; requires MRI topography pattern recognition, complete TOAST-classification embolic workup exclusion, and integration of family history with imaging to reach CADASIL diagnosis; mechanism-specific genetic testing required as load-bearing action.
